leads.name: The Persian Ironwood of Artis

location.address: Artis Park, Plantage Kerklaan 38-40, 1018 CZ Amsterdam

leads.story: Artis keeps more than eight hundred trees across two hundred species, and the man who looks after them picks this one. Jan de Jong, the park's tree specialist, calls the Persian ironwood his favourite and describes it as warrig en grillig, tangled and irregular, which undersells it. The species does something few trees do: branches that touch as they grow fuse into each other, so an old ironwood ends up as one knotted structure rather than a trunk with limbs hanging off it. The bark flakes away in plates like a plane tree's, leaving patches of grey, green and brown. Amsterdam's register of protected trees carries it as N1763, planted in 1910, trunk 205 centimetres around. That makes it barely a century old, young next to the oak thirty metres away, which took root around 1750 and is the oldest tree in the city. The two are an easy walk apart, past the giant tortoises, and together they explain what Artis is: a zoo laid out in 1838 by a society that collected plants as seriously as animals, with the trees part of the plan rather than scenery added afterwards. In late autumn this one carries red, orange and purple in the same crown at the same time. Entry is a zoo ticket.

best_time.label: late October into November, when red, orange and purple appear in the same crown

leads.name: The Coast Redwood of Artis

location.address: Artis Park, Plantage Kerklaan 38-40, 1018 CZ Amsterdam

leads.story: The tallest tree species on earth has a specimen standing beside a planetarium in central Amsterdam. Coast redwoods pass 110 metres in the fog belt of northern California, where they take a serious share of their water straight out of sea mist. This one grows about nine thousand kilometres from there, on drained peat, at a latitude California never reaches. Amsterdam's register of protected trees lists it as N5627, planted circa 1920, and the circa is the register's own hedge rather than ours. The trunk is 271 centimetres around. A century in, it is a juvenile: coast redwoods routinely run past a thousand years, and the oldest known are more than twice that. The bark gives the species away when the shape does not. It is thick, fibrous and reddish, soft enough to press a thumb into, and it is what lets the tree shrug off the fires that clear out everything else on a Californian forest floor. There is no fire here and no fog, only a Dutch zoo that started planting exotics in the nineteenth century and then kept them. It is evergreen, so no month shows it better than another. The Persian ironwood and the Heimanseik, the oldest tree in Amsterdam, are both a few minutes away on the same walk. Entry is an Artis ticket.

leads.name: The Twisted Catalpa of the Hortus

location.address: Hortus Botanicus Amsterdam, Plantage Middenlaan 2A, 1018 DD Amsterdam

leads.story: The trunk turns as it rises, a slow corkscrew that the national guide to Amsterdam's monumental trees singles out as the reason to stop. This is a southern catalpa, native to a small pocket of the southeastern United States and far more common in European gardens than in its own range. The city register has it as N1776, planted in 1910, trunk 318 centimetres around; the Bomenstichting guide puts the planting somewhere between 1910 and 1920 and measures the same three metres, which is about as close as two independent sources ever get. Dutch has two names for the species and both are literal: trompetboom, trumpet tree, for the cream and yellow flowers with speckled throats that cover it in July, and bonenboom, bean tree, for the long thin seed pods that hang on through winter and rattle. The leaves are the size of a spread hand. The same guide adds that catalpas keep mosquitoes and flies at a distance, which is not the worst property for a garden on the edge of the Plantage canals. The Hortus Botanicus has grown plants on this ground since 1638, so the catalpa arrived when the garden was already 270 years old and still counts as one of its younger residents. Entry needs a Hortus ticket.

leads.name: The Shellbark Hickory of the Hortus
leads.age_estimate: roughly 76 to 114 years (sources disagree on planting year)

location.address: Hortus Botanicus Amsterdam, Plantage Middenlaan 2A, 1018 DD Amsterdam

leads.story: The Dutch tree foundation calls this the oldest shellbark hickory in the Netherlands. The city of Amsterdam records it as planted in 1950, which would rule that out. Both are describing the same tree in the same corner of the Hortus, and they disagree by thirty-eight years: the Bomenstichting guide gives 1912, the municipal register N1768 gives 1950 along with a trunk 251 centimetres around. Nothing available settles it, so the honest age is somewhere between seventy-five and a hundred and fifteen years, and the claim to be the country's oldest only stands under the earlier date. The species is not in doubt, and it barely exists here. Shellbark hickory comes from the wet river bottoms of the American Midwest, is a close relative of the pecan, and drops round nuts inside a thick green husk that looks poisonous and is not: the kernel is sweet and takes real work to reach. The bark is where the name comes from, peeling off the trunk in long curling plates that stay attached at both ends. Crush a leaf and it smells sharply of walnut. A few paths away stands a Turkish hazel that the same foundation calls the oldest and thickest in the country, so this corner of the Plantage has a habit of holding records it cannot quite prove. Entry needs a Hortus ticket.

leads.name: The Ginkgo of the Hortus
leads.age_estimate: roughly 96 to 136 years (sources disagree, and the exact specimen match is uncertain)

location.address: Hortus Botanicus Amsterdam, Plantage Middenlaan 2A, 1018 DD Amsterdam

leads.story: Ginkgo is the only surviving species of an entire order of plants, a lineage already old when the first dinosaurs appeared and one that outlived them by sixty-six million years. Everything else on that branch has been a fossil since the Jurassic. Which particular trunk this entry points at is less certain than the biology. The Bomenstichting guide records a monumental ginkgo in the Hortus planted between 1890 and 1900. Amsterdam's own register lists two ginkgos here, fifteen metres apart, both dated 1930. The pin sits on the thicker of the pair, N1771, at 321 centimetres around, because girth is a better guide to age than a register date, but nothing so far proves the two sources describe the same tree. Read the location as this corner of the garden rather than one exact trunk, and the age as somewhere between ninety-five and a hundred and thirty-five years. Come in November. Ginkgo leaves are small stiff fans, they turn a flat uniform gold rather than the mottled reds of everything around them, and then the tree lets almost all of them go within a couple of days, so the ground underneath goes yellow at once. Entry needs a Hortus ticket.

leads.name: The Weteringplantsoen Wych Elm

location.address: Weteringplantsoen achter het Van Randwijk-monument, Amsterdam

leads.story:
Nobody knows when this elm was planted and the register says so outright: history unknown, planting somewhere between 1900 and 1910. What is documented is what stands in front of it. The Van Randwijk monument on the Weteringplantsoen carries the best known line in Dutch resistance writing, Henk van Randwijk's warning that a people which yields to tyrants will lose more than life and property, and then the light goes out. Van Randwijk edited the underground paper Vrij Nederland through the occupation.

The tree behind the monument is a wych elm, and that is the interesting part of the label. Ulmus glabra is usually counted as the only elm truly native to the Netherlands, and it is highly susceptible to Dutch elm disease, which arrived in the 1920s and worked through the country for the rest of the century. A mature wych elm standing in a Dutch city centre is not a common thing. This one is around 120 years old, so it was here before either world war and has stood through both.

It sits in a strip of grass and gravel between the Weteringschans and the water, the sort of triangle a city ends up with where two roads fail to meet cleanly. Free, always open, and a few minutes' walk from the Rijksmuseum. Three more trees on this list stand within two minutes of it.

leads.name: The Weteringplantsoen Ginkgo
leads.story:
There is a ginkgo growing on a traffic island on the Weteringschans, and it is the least likely thing on this list. The species is around 200 million years old, older than the flowering plants, and it survives in the wild in a handful of Chinese valleys. Its Dutch name, tempelboom, records how it got through: monks planted it in temple grounds and kept it going while it disappeared everywhere else. This one lives between lanes of traffic.

Amsterdam put it in somewhere between 1910 and 1920 and the register records no history for it whatsoever, which suits a tree that simply gets on with things. Ginkgo tolerates exactly the conditions that kill other street trees: compacted soil, road salt, exhaust, root space measured in single square metres. Several ginkgos within two kilometres of the Hiroshima hypocentre survived the bomb and are still growing.

Come in November. For eleven months this is a green tree with odd fan-shaped leaves that people walk past without a glance. Then over about a week the whole crown turns a flat saturated gold, and then it drops the lot, often in a day or two, leaving a gold ring on the tarmac around it. Traffic islands rarely get a moment like that.

Free, always visible, and easy to miss for most of the year. The wych elm, the leaning poplar and the plane are all a minute or two away.

leads.name: The Wertheimpark Sycamore
leads.story:
A sycamore is the most ordinary large tree in northern Europe, which makes it worth asking why this one sits on the national register for dendrological reasons rather than for history or memorial value. The register does not say. Under history it writes: unknown. Somebody with a measuring tape decided this specimen was exceptional enough to protect and left it at that.

It stands behind the monument to Abraham Carel Wertheim, the banker and philanthropist the park was named after in 1898, a year after his death. The tree went in between 1910 and 1920, so it is around 110 years old and has spent every year of it a few metres behind that monument.

Acer pseudoplatanus is a maple that acquired the English name sycamore, which it shares with an unrelated American plane, and the confusion has never been cleared up. It seeds itself into every gap in every European city, grows anywhere, and if nothing interferes it can pass four hundred years, which makes 110 barely adulthood. The species is so common that a good specimen tends to be overlooked, which is roughly what happened here until the register caught up with it.

Free, in a park of three quarters of a hectare holding around fifteen trees over a century old. Go and see whether you can work out what the surveyor saw.

leads.name: The White Poplar of Broersepark
leads.age_estimate: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870

location.address: Aan de vijver zuidzijde Broersepark, Amstelveen

leads.story:
The register that protects this poplar says plainly that it is no longer impressive. Its own entry drops the word monumental and then keeps the tree on the list for one reason: with a planting recorded between 1860 and 1870, it is probably the oldest thing growing in the Broersepark.

The park in Amstelveen is much younger than that. It was designed in 1926 and laid out over the following years as a Wandelpark, a place made for walking, and only in 1967 took the name of Chris P. Broerse, the garden man who had worked there since the first season. On the dates in its file the poplar was already sixty years old before anyone drew a line on the plan. Nobody wrote down who put it there.

It wears the years openly. The crown has been knocked about, the trunk leans, and the root plate has lifted enough to raise a hump at the foot. In 1999 honey fungus, a wood-rotting parasite, turned up at the base, and the condition has been rated moderate ever since. What it still does as well as anything younger is the trick white poplars are named for: a gust turns the leaves over and the whole crown flickers silver.

You will find it on the south side of the park, at the edge of the pond. Only the national register describes this tree, so if you know more of its story, tell us.

leads.name: The Poplar of the Eleanor Rooseveltlaan
leads.age_estimate: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting date around 1910

location.address: Voor makelaarskantoor,Eleanor Rooseveltlaan 255, straat van messina, Amstelveen

leads.story:
Hardly anyone lets a Canadian poplar reach this age. The register puts this one's planting between 1900 and 1910, which makes it about 120, and the species is normally out of the ground long before that.

Populus x canadensis is a hybrid of an American poplar and a European one, bred for speed, and it went into the Dutch landscape in enormous numbers along roads, dykes and field edges. It makes height in a decade and shelter in two. What it does not make is old bones: the wood is soft, heavy limbs come out in a gale, and most street poplars are taken down at fifty or sixty on exactly that reasoning. This one is still standing in a strip of municipal garden on the Eleanor Rooseveltlaan in Amstelveen. Roosevelt herself was a young woman in New York when it was planted.

The register knows nothing else about it. Under the tree's own history it records a single word: unknown. Nobody wrote down who put it there, or why a fast nursery hybrid on a suburban corner was left alone long enough to end up on a national list of monumental trees. If you know that story, tell us.

Come on a windy day. Poplar leaves hang on flattened stalks that let them twist edge-on to a gust, so a crown this size does not rustle so much as pour.

leads.name: The Elm of Elsenhoeve
leads.age_estimate: roughly 100 years, from a registered planting date around 1930
leads.story:
This elm is alive because somebody injects it, every year. The register's entire note on the tree is one line of Dutch saying exactly that: treated annually against elm disease.

Dutch elm disease emptied European streets of a tree that used to define them. The fungus travels from tree to tree in bark beetles and can wilt a mature elm within a season. It is named after the Netherlands not because it began here but because Dutch scientists were the ones who identified the fungus, in the 1920s, which is roughly when this tree went into the ground: the register puts its planting between 1920 and 1930. It has lived its whole life alongside the thing that kills its kind, through a century in which most of Europe's elms disappeared.

Ulmus x hollandica is a natural hybrid, wych elm crossed with field elm, and the Amsterdam region is one of the few places in Europe where elms are still an ordinary street tree rather than a rescued specimen. That took decades of felling infected wood, watching for beetles, and precisely the treatment this one gets.

It stands in front of Speelboerderij Elsenhoeve, a children's farm on the Bankrasweg in Amstelveen, so most of the people underneath it are five years old and looking at goats. The pin marks the garden rather than the trunk, and only the national register describes this tree, so if you know more of it, tell us.

leads.name: The Red Horse Chestnut of Wilhelminaplein
leads.age_estimate: roughly 100 years, from a registered planting date around 1930
leads.story:
Half of this tree is American. The red horse chestnut is a cross between the white-flowered chestnut of every Dutch avenue and Aesculus pavia, a red-flowered species from the American southeast, and it turns up in the record in Germany around 1820 with nobody quite able to say who made it.

The result is the best-behaved chestnut on any street. In May it holds up candles of deep rose-pink rather than white, a little later than its white parent, so a street planted with both appears to flower twice. It sets very few conkers, and the husks it does set have almost no spines, which makes it a disappointing tree for anyone under twelve. In exchange it largely escapes the leaf miner moth that has been browning out Dutch horse chestnuts by August for twenty years now; the caterpillars strongly prefer the white parent, and this hybrid stays green into autumn while its neighbours look scorched.

This one stands in public planting on the Wilhelminaplein in Amstelveen, with a registered planting somewhere between 1920 and 1930, which puts it at roughly a century old. That is all anybody has written down. The national register's history field for this tree is blank, and no second source describes it at all. If you know who planted it, or what for, tell us and we will add it.
